procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 18, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1642 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Municipal Board of Saharanpur appealed to the High Court under s. 417(3), Cr. P.C. against the trial court's acquittal of the accused. The High Court allowed the appeal, disagreeing with the trial court and convicting the appellant. The High Court subsequently dismissed an application by the accused under s. 561(A), Cr. P.C. for reviewing its judgment and refused a certificate under Art. 134 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused appealed to the Supreme Court after obtaining special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated April 18, 1966.

directions: The appellant should surrender to his bail.
The appellant should serve the sentence imposed on him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appeal filed by the Municipal Board in the High Court was maintainable, given that the complaint was signed by the Food Inspector and not the Board itself.

facts: A complaint was filed against the accused, purportedly by the Municipal Board, but it was signed by its Food Inspector.
The trial court acquitted the accused.
The Municipal Board appealed this acquittal to the High Court, which convicted the accused.
The accused never challenged the authority of the Food Inspector to file the complaint on behalf of the Board, either in the trial court or during the High Court appeal hearing.
The accused raised the issue of the appeal's maintainability for the first time only after the High Court had already delivered its judgment.
law: Under Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, a local authority (like the Municipal Board) is competent to file a complaint.
A local authority can also authorize a person, such as a Food Inspector, to file a complaint on its behalf.
A complaint filed by an officer on the authority of a local board is legally considered to have been instituted by the board itself.
Under Section 417(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, only the complainant can appeal an order of acquittal.
application: The Court reasoned that if the Food Inspector was authorized by the Municipal Board, then the Board was legally the complainant.
The question of whether the Food Inspector was actually authorized is a question of fact.

Crucially, the accused never challenged the Food Inspector's authority during the trial or the appeal. All parties and lower courts proceeded on the basis that the complaint was validly instituted by the Board.
The Court held that the accused could not be permitted to raise this factual challenge for the first time after the appeal had already been decided.
The Court presumed that the official act of filing the complaint was done lawfully, especially since it was not challenged earlier.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention. It held that because the complaint was legally considered to have been instituted by the Municipal Board (a fact that went unchallenged), the Board was the proper complainant. As the complainant, the Board was competent to file the appeal against the acquittal, and therefore, the appeal was maintainable.

issue.issue_text: Whether the question of the Food Inspector's authority to file the complaint, being a question of fact, could be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.

facts: The appellant (the accused) did not raise any objection regarding the Food Inspector's authority to file the complaint in either the trial court or the High Court.
Both the lower courts and the parties involved proceeded on the assumption that the complaint was validly instituted by the Municipal Board, with the Food Inspector acting on its behalf.
The appellant raised this objection for the first time only after the High Court had disposed of the appeal.
law: The question of whether the Food Inspector was authorized by the Municipal Board to file the complaint is a question of fact.
A question of fact cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court; it must be put into issue at the trial court level.
Official acts are presumed to have been done according to law unless challenged.
application: The Court reasoned that if the accused had challenged the Food Inspector's authority at trial, the trial court would have investigated that factual question.
Since the issue was never raised, all parties proceeded on the basis that the complaint was valid.
The Court concluded that the accused could not be permitted to raise this new factual contention for the first time after the appeal had already been decided by the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's attempt to question the Food Inspector's authority because it was a question of fact that was not raised in the lower courts and therefore could not be entertained for the first time at the Supreme Court level.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be convicted on the strength of the Public Analyst's certificate, which was alleged to not contain the data for the conclusion.

facts: The appellant contended that he could not be convicted because the Public Analyst's report did not contain the data on which the analyst's conclusion was based.
law: The Supreme Court held that a Public Analyst's report does not need to contain the 'mode or particulars of analysis or the test applied'.
However, the report must contain the 'result of analysis, namely, data from which it can be inferred whether the article of food was or was not adulterated'.
application: The Court reviewed the report in this specific case and found that the appellant's claim was factually incorrect.
It determined that the report did, in fact, contain the relevant data on which the analyst came to his conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that since the analyst's report contained the necessary data to infer adulteration, it provided a valid basis for the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appeal filed by the Municipal Board in the High Court was maintainable, given that the complaint was signed by the Food Inspector and not the Board itself.
appellant_arguments: The appeal filed by the Municipal Board in the High Court was not maintainable under s. 417(3), Cr. P.C.
This is because the complaint was instituted by the Food Inspector, not the Municipal Board, and therefore the Board was not the 'complainant' entitled to file an appeal against acquittal.
respondent_arguments: Under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, it was competent for the Municipal Board to authorize the Food Inspector to file the complaint.
A complaint filed by an authorized officer of a local authority is, in law, a complaint instituted by that authority itself.
Therefore, the Municipal Board was the legal complainant and had the right to file the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the question of the Food Inspector's authority to file the complaint, being a question of fact, could be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
appellant_arguments: Permission to file a complaint under s. 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is a condition precedent for a valid complaint, and its fulfillment must be proven for the court to have jurisdiction.
As it is a question of jurisdiction, it can be raised at any stage, even for the first time in the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The question of whether the Food Inspector was specifically authorized by the Board is a question of fact.
This factual question was never put into issue by the appellant in the trial court or the High Court.
The appellant cannot be permitted to raise a question of fact for the first time at this late stage, especially after the appeal has been disposed of.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be convicted on the strength of the Public Analyst's certificate, which was alleged to not contain the data for the conclusion.
appellant_arguments: The report of the Public Analyst could not be a valid basis for conviction because it did not contain the data on which the analyst's conclusion was based.
Without the underlying data, the court cannot verify the analyst's conclusion that the food was adulterated.
respondent_arguments: The analyst's report did contain the necessary data to support the conclusion.
The report provided a sufficient basis for the conviction.

cases.case_name: Nagar Mahapalika of Kanpur v. Sri Ram
cases.principle: The report of a public analyst under s. 13 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 need not contain the mode or particulars of analysis, but must contain data from which it can be inferred whether the article of food was or was not adulterated as defined in s. 2(1) of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Public Analyst's report can form a valid basis for a conviction if it contains the data from which it can be inferred whether an article of food was adulterated as defined in the Act. Additionally, a complaint filed by a Food Inspector on the authority of a Municipal Board is considered to have been instituted by the Board itself.
obiter: The question of whether a Food Inspector was properly authorized to file a complaint is a question of fact that cannot be raised for the first time on appeal if it was not put into issue in the lower courts.

There is no analogy between the section authorizing a complaint and provisions requiring sanction for the institution of criminal proceedings, as the former is a conferment of authority that can be granted long before a specific offense occurs.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court upheld the appellant's conviction, finding that the appeal filed by the Municipal Board in the High Court was maintainable because a complaint filed by an authorized Food Inspector is legally considered a complaint by the Board itself. The Court refused to entertain the appellant's challenge to the Food Inspector's authority, deeming it a question of fact that was impermissibly raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level. Finally, the Court concluded that the Public Analyst's report provided a valid basis for the conviction as it contained the necessary data from which adulteration could be inferred.
legal_tests_applied: A Public Analyst's report is legally sufficient if it contains 'the result of analysis, namely, data from which it can be inferred whether the anicle of food was or was not adulterated,' and it is not necessary for it to contain the mode or particulars of the analysis or the tests applied.

The question of whether a Food Inspector was specifically authorized by a local board to file a complaint is a question of fact, not jurisdiction, and cannot be raised for the first time at the final appellate stage.

An authorization to file a complaint under s. 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is a general conferment of authority and does not require the sanctioning authority to apply its mind to the specific facts of a case, unlike other types of statutory sanctions.
The presumption that 'Official acts must be deemed to have been done according to law' applies unless the authority for such acts is challenged at the trial court level.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the Municipal Board could not appeal was rejected because the court held that if a complaint is filed by a Food Inspector on the authority of the Board, 'the complaint must be held to have been instituted by the local board itself.'

The appellant was barred from challenging the Food Inspector's authority because it was a question of fact that was 'never put into issue' in the lower courts, and the appellant 'cannot be permitted to take up that contention for the first time after the disposal of the appeal.'

The argument that the analyst's report was an invalid basis for conviction was dismissed because the court found it was 'not correct to say that the repon does not contain the data on the basis of which the analyst came to his conclusion. The relevant data is given in the repon.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position on the maintainability of the appeal was accepted because a complaint filed by an authorized officer of a local authority is, in law, a complaint instituted by that authority, making the Municipal Board the proper complainant with the right to appeal.

The respondent successfully argued against the belated challenge to the Inspector's authority, as the court agreed it was a question of fact that should have been raised in the trial court, where the prosecution would have had the opportunity to prove it.

The respondent's reliance on the Public Analyst's report was affirmed, as the court found it met the legal standard by containing sufficient data to support the conclusion of adulteration, referencing a similar report that it had previously held to be sufficient.
policy_considerations: The court's refusal to allow a question of fact to be raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level ensures finality and prevents parties from strategically withholding objections until the final stage of litigation, which would undermine the judicial process.

By presuming that official acts are done lawfully unless challenged, the court avoids placing an undue burden on the prosecution to prove every procedural step when it is not contested by the defense at the appropriate time.
